objectives: Students will read data tables and bar and line graphs by checking the title, labels, units, and key.
Students will calculate the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set and explain what each measure shows.

teach:
Week 2 Science: Working with Data — Tables, Graphs, Mean, Median, Mode, Range, Units, and Probability

Objectives

  • Read data tables and bar and line graphs accurately by checking the title, column headings, axis labels, units, and key.
  • Calculate the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set and explain what each one tells us.
  • Recognize an outlier and decide whether the mean or the median better describes typical data.
  • Calculate rates of change from a table or graph and convert between common science units.
  • Find simple probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percents, and use them to predict expected outcomes.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors.
  • Calculator for each student (a basic or scientific calculator; an on-screen calculator is available on the GED Science test).
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • Scratch paper for organizing data in order from least to greatest.
  • This week's 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Rain gauge data: total, greatest day, and a first look at "typical."
Direct instruction20Reading tables and graphs; mean, median, mode, range; outliers; rates and units; probability. Worked Examples 1–4.
Guided practice15Stream field data: students compute and interpret with teacher support.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket, study plan, and this week's Practice GED.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Put this table on the board and ask students to answer the three questions on scratch paper.

DayMonTueWedThuFri
Rainfall in garden gauge (mm)301250
  1. How much rain fell in all five days?
  2. Which day had the most rain?
  3. If you had to give one number for a "typical" day, what would you say?

Answers: (1) 3 + 0 + 12 + 5 + 0 = 20 mm. (2) Wednesday, 12 mm. (3) Accept any reasoned answer, then use it as a hook: the mean is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 mm, but the median (middle value of 0, 0, 3, 5, 12) is 3 mm and the mode is 0 mm. Ask: "Why do we get three different 'typical' values?" Today's lesson answers that question.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. Read before you calculate. Most data mistakes on the GED come from misreading, not from bad arithmetic. Teach the routine T-A-U-K: read the Title (what the data are about), the Axes or column headings (what was measured), the Units (cm, mm, °C, mg/L, beats per minute), and the Key (which bar or line is which). Students should say in one sentence what the table or graph shows before they answer anything.

2. Pick the right graph.

  • Bar graphs compare separate categories (number of each tree species, rainfall in four cities).
  • Line graphs show how one quantity changes over time or as another quantity changes continuously (a patient's temperature each hour, plant height each week).
  • Recall from Week 1: the independent variable goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis.

On a line graph, a trend is the overall direction: increasing, decreasing, or no clear pattern. A steeper section means a faster change.

3. Measures of center and spread. Write these on the board and keep them up for the whole lesson.

Mean (average) = sum of the values ÷ number of values.

Median = middle value after putting the data in order. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

Mode = the value that occurs most often. A data set can have one mode, more than one, or none.

Range = greatest value − least value. It measures spread, not center.

4. Outliers. An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. It may be a real but unusual result, or an error (a misread instrument, a contaminated sample). Outliers pull the mean strongly toward them but barely move the median. So when a data set has an outlier, the median usually describes a "typical" value better.

5. Rates and units. A rate compares two quantities with different units: cm per day, beats per minute, km per hour. To find an average rate of change from a table or graph:

Rate of change = (change in the y-value) ÷ (change in the x-value) = (ending value − starting value) ÷ (ending time − starting time).

Unit conversions: multiply when going from a larger unit to a smaller one (1 m = 100 cm, 1 L = 1,000 mL, 1 kg = 1,000 g, 1 hour = 60 minutes), and divide when going from a smaller unit to a larger one. Always write the unit with every answer.

6. Probability. Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

P(event) = (number of favorable outcomes) ÷ (total number of possible outcomes)
P(event does not happen) = 1 − P(event)
Expected number = probability × number of trials

Show that 1/4 = 0.25 = 25% are the same probability. A weather forecast of "30% chance of rain" means a probability of 0.30 of rain, so the chance of no rain is 70%. Experimental probability comes from data that were actually collected; theoretical probability comes from reasoning about equally likely outcomes (a fair coin, a number cube).

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Center and spread (health). A nurse records the resting heart rates of six adults, in beats per minute (bpm): 62, 68, 58, 74, 70, 88. Find the mean, median, mode, and range.

Mean: 62 + 68 + 58 + 74 + 70 + 88 = 420. Then 420 ÷ 6 = 70 bpm.

Median: Put the values in order: 58, 62, 68, 70, 74, 88. There are six values, so the two middle values are 68 and 70. (68 + 70) ÷ 2 = 138 ÷ 2 = 69 bpm.

Mode: No value appears more than once, so there is no mode.

Range: 88 − 58 = 30 bpm.

Teaching point: Ordering the data is the step students skip. The median of the unordered list would wrongly be (58 + 74) ÷ 2 = 66.

Worked Example 2: An outlier (experiment). A student counts bacteria colonies on five plates that were treated the same way: 41, 44, 39, 42, 104. She notes that plate 5 was left uncovered for an hour.

Mean with all five plates: 41 + 44 + 39 + 42 + 104 = 270. Then 270 ÷ 5 = 54 colonies.

Median with all five plates: In order: 39, 41, 42, 44, 104. The middle value is 42 colonies.

Mean without plate 5: 41 + 44 + 39 + 42 = 166. Then 166 ÷ 4 = 41.5 colonies.

Interpretation: The single value of 104 raised the mean from 41.5 to 54, which is higher than four of the five plates. The median (42) stayed close to the typical plate. Because plate 5 was likely contaminated, the student has a good reason to treat 104 as an outlier and report the median or the mean without it.

Worked Example 3: Rate of change and units (field data). A student measures the height of a sunflower every two weeks.

Week02468
Height (cm)820386280

(a) During which two-week period did the plant grow fastest? Find each change: 20 − 8 = 12; 38 − 20 = 18; 62 − 38 = 24; 80 − 62 = 18. The largest change is 24 cm, from week 4 to week 6. (On a line graph, that is the steepest segment.)

(b) What was the average growth rate from week 2 to week 6? (62 − 20) ÷ (6 − 2) = 42 ÷ 4 = 10.5 cm per week.

(c) Express that rate in millimeters per day. There are 7 days in a week: 10.5 ÷ 7 = 1.5 cm per day. There are 10 mm in 1 cm: 1.5 × 10 = 15 mm per day.

Worked Example 4: Probability from field data. A biologist sets 50 small-animal traps in a meadow. The next morning, 18 traps hold a mouse, 7 hold a vole, and 25 are empty.

(a) Probability that a trap caught a mouse: 18 ÷ 50 = 0.36 = 36% (or 9/25).

(b) Probability that a trap caught any animal: (18 + 7) ÷ 50 = 25 ÷ 50 = 1/2, or 50%.

(c) Probability that a trap did not catch a mouse: 1 − 0.36 = 0.64, or 64%.

(d) If the biologist sets 200 traps under the same conditions, about how many will catch a mouse? Expected number = 0.36 × 200 = 72 traps.

Teaching point: 72 is an expected value, not a guarantee. Real results will vary a little from trial to trial.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Display this field data table. Students work in pairs; pause after each question to discuss.

Stream siteWater temperature (°C)Dissolved oxygen (mg/L)
A1410.2
B188.9
C169.6
D208.1
  1. What is the mean water temperature?
  2. What is the median dissolved oxygen level?
  3. What is the range of the dissolved oxygen levels?
  4. Describe the relationship between temperature and dissolved oxygen.
  5. Convert the temperature at Site D to degrees Fahrenheit using °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32.
  6. If one site is chosen at random, what is the probability its dissolved oxygen is above 9 mg/L?

1. 14 + 18 + 16 + 20 = 68; 68 ÷ 4 = 17 °C.

2. In order: 8.1, 8.9, 9.6, 10.2. Middle two: (8.9 + 9.6) ÷ 2 = 18.5 ÷ 2 = 9.25 mg/L.

3. 10.2 − 8.1 = 2.1 mg/L.

4. Reorder by temperature: 14 °C (10.2), 16 °C (9.6), 18 °C (8.9), 20 °C (8.1). As water temperature increases, dissolved oxygen decreases. Remind students the table shows a pattern among four sites; it does not by itself prove temperature is the cause.

5. 20 × 9/5 = 36; 36 + 32 = 68 °F.

6. Sites A (10.2) and C (9.6) are above 9. P = 2/4 = 1/2, or 50%.

Checks for Understanding

  • "Which measure would change the most if we added one very large value: mean, median, or mode?" Expected: the mean.
  • "Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 1." Expected: order 1, 3, 7, 9; (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.
  • "A forecast gives a 15% chance of frost. What is the chance of no frost?" Expected: 85%.
  • "How many milliliters are in 2.4 liters?" Expected: 2.4 × 1,000 = 2,400 mL.
  • "On a line graph, how can you spot the time when change was fastest without calculating?" Expected: find the steepest segment.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Finding the median without ordering the data. Correction: require students to rewrite the list in order and cross off one value from each end until they reach the middle.

Confusing range with a measure of center. Students report the range as the "typical" value. Correction: range answers "how spread out?" Mean, median, and mode answer "what is typical?"

Reading the wrong row, column, or line. Correction: use the T-A-U-K routine and have students place a finger or cursor on the row and column heading before reading a value.

Dropping or mixing units. A rate of "10.5" means nothing without "cm per week." Correction: write units on every line of work, and check whether an answer choice uses different units than the data.

Dividing in the wrong order for a rate or probability. Correction: say the rate in words first ("centimeters per week" means cm ÷ weeks), and for probability always put the total on the bottom.

Treating expected outcomes as guaranteed, or extending a trend too far. Correction: use "about" with expected values, and do not predict far beyond the range of data that were collected.

Differentiation

Support: Give a fill-in frame for each measure ("Sum = ____; number of values = ____; mean = ____ ÷ ____ = ____"). Start with odd-sized data sets for the median before moving to even-sized sets. Let students keep the Study Notes formula box out during practice, and have them highlight units in every table before they begin.

Stretch: (1) Ask students to build a data set of five values whose mean is 10 and whose median is 8 (one answer: 4, 6, 8, 12, 20; sum 50, mean 10, middle value 8). (2) Introduce two independent events: if each seed has a 0.8 probability of sprouting, the probability that both of two seeds sprout is 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. (3) Have students explain why a mean of trials is more reliable than a single trial.

How This Shows Up on the GED

Data questions appear throughout the GED Science test. Many stimuli include a table or graph from an experiment, a field study, weather records, or a health study. Expect wording like:

  • "What is the mean of the three trials for the 40 °C group?"
  • "Based on the graph, between which two times did the temperature change the most?"
  • "Which statement is supported by the data in the table?"
  • "What is the probability that …? Express your answer as a percent."
  • "About how many … would be expected in a sample of 500?"

Formats include multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank (typing a number such as a mean or a rate), drop-down menus that complete a statement with a value or a unit, drag-and-drop sorting, and select-two items that ask which statements the data support. An on-screen calculator is available on the Science test, but students still need to know which calculation to do. Train this routine: (1) read the title, labels, and units; (2) restate what the data show in one sentence; (3) decide which calculation the question asks for; (4) check the answer against the data and its units.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding above, then preview the exit ticket, the study plan, and this week's Practice GED.
student:
Working with Data in Science

Scientists collect numbers: temperatures, heights, heart rates, counts of animals. On the GED Science test, many questions give you a table or graph and ask what the data show. You will not need advanced math. You need to read carefully, choose the right calculation, and keep track of units. This lesson shows you how.

1. Read the table or graph first

Before you answer any question, check four things. A handy way to remember them is T-A-U-K:

  • Title: What is this about?
  • Axes or column headings: What was measured?
  • Units: Centimeters? Degrees? Beats per minute?
  • Key: If there are two bars or lines, which is which?

Bar graphs compare separate groups, like rainfall in four cities. Line graphs show change over time, like a plant's height each week. On a line graph, the trend is the overall direction. The steeper the line, the faster the change.

2. Mean, median, mode, and range

MeasureHow to find itWhat it tells you
MeanAdd all values, then divide by how many there are.The average
MedianPut values in order; take the middle one. If there are two middle values, find their mean.The middle
ModeFind the value that appears most often.The most common value
RangeGreatest value minus least value.How spread out the data are

Example 1. A sleep study records how many hours six people slept: 7.5, 6, 8, 5.5, 6, 9.

Mean: 7.5 + 6 + 8 + 5.5 + 6 + 9 = 42. Then 42 ÷ 6 = 7 hours.

Median: In order: 5.5, 6, 6, 7.5, 8, 9. The two middle values are 6 and 7.5. (6 + 7.5) ÷ 2 = 13.5 ÷ 2 = 6.75 hours.

Mode: 6 appears twice. Mode = 6 hours.

Range: 9 − 5.5 = 3.5 hours.

3. Watch for outliers

An outlier is a value far away from the others. It might be a real, unusual result or a mistake. An outlier pulls the mean toward it, but it hardly changes the median.

Example 2. Five students time how long a cup of ice takes to melt (minutes): 30, 32, 29, 31, 78. One cup was left in the shade by accident.

Mean: 30 + 32 + 29 + 31 + 78 = 200. Then 200 ÷ 5 = 40 minutes. That is longer than four of the five cups!

Median: In order: 29, 30, 31, 32, 78. The middle value is 31 minutes, which is much closer to a typical cup.

When there is an outlier, the median usually describes the typical value better.

Tip: Range is not an "average." It tells you how spread out the data are. If a question asks what is typical, think mean, median, or mode.

4. Rates and units

A rate compares two different units, such as centimeters per day or beats per minute. The word "per" means "divide."

Rate of change = (change in amount) ÷ (change in time)

Example 3. At 6:00 a.m. the air temperature was 52 °F. At 12:00 noon it was 70 °F. What was the average rate of warming?

Change in temperature: 70 − 52 = 18 °F. Change in time: 12 − 6 = 6 hours.

Rate: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 °F per hour.

Science uses the metric system. The most common conversions:

LengthVolumeMassTime
1 cm = 10 mm
1 m = 100 cm
1 km = 1,000 m		1 L = 1,000 mL1 kg = 1,000 g
1 g = 1,000 mg		1 min = 60 s
1 h = 60 min

Going from a big unit to a small unit, multiply. Going from a small unit to a big unit, divide.

Example 4. A doctor tells a patient to drink 1.5 L of water a day. A glass holds 250 mL. How many glasses is that?

Convert liters to milliliters (big to small, so multiply): 1.5 × 1,000 = 1,500 mL.

Divide by the glass size: 1,500 ÷ 250 = 6 glasses.

5. Probability

Probability tells how likely something is. It is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). You can write it as a fraction, a decimal, or a percent.

P(event) = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes
P(not the event) = 1 − P(event)
Expected number = probability × number of tries

Example 5. In a bird survey, volunteers counted 40 birds: 14 sparrows, 10 robins, and 16 other birds.

Probability that a counted bird was a robin: 10 ÷ 40 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

Probability that it was not a robin: 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, or 75%.

If the next survey counts 200 birds in the same place, about how many robins are expected? 0.25 × 200 = about 50 robins.

Tip: A weather forecast of "40% chance of rain" means the probability of rain is 0.40. The chance of no rain is 100% − 40% = 60%.

Try It

1. A plant lost these amounts of water on four days (mL): 12, 15, 9, 14. What is the mean?

Show answer

12 + 15 + 9 + 14 = 50. 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 mL.

2. Find the median and the range of these rainfall amounts (cm): 3, 8, 1, 6, 4.

Show answer

In order: 1, 3, 4, 6, 8. Median = 4 cm. Range = 8 − 1 = 7 cm.

3. A runner drinks 0.75 L of a sports drink. How many milliliters is that?

Show answer

Big unit to small unit, so multiply: 0.75 × 1,000 = 750 mL.

4. A forecast says there is a 20% chance of snow tomorrow. What is the probability that it will not snow?

Show answer

100% − 20% = 80% (or 0.8).

5. A fair number cube has sides 1 through 6. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?

Show answer

Favorable outcomes: 5 and 6, so 2 outcomes out of 6. P = 2/6 = 1/3 (about 33%).
post:
Post Lesson: Working with Data

Summary of Key Points

  • Before calculating, read the title, axes or headings, units, and key (T-A-U-K).
  • Bar graphs compare categories. Line graphs show change over time; the steepest part shows the fastest change.
  • Mean = sum ÷ count. Median = middle value of the ordered data. Mode = most frequent value. Range = greatest − least.
  • An outlier pulls the mean toward it; the median is more resistant, so it often describes typical data better.
  • A rate is change in amount ÷ change in time. Always keep units, and multiply to go from larger to smaller metric units.
  • Probability = favorable ÷ total, from 0 to 1. P(not) = 1 − P. Expected number = probability × number of tries.

Exit Ticket

1. Find the mean of 4, 7, and 10.

Show answer

4 + 7 + 10 = 21; 21 ÷ 3 = 7.

2. Find the median of 2, 9, 5, 11.

Show answer

In order: 2, 5, 9, 11. Middle values 5 and 9: (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7.

3. One very large value is added to a data set. Which measure changes the most: the mean or the median?

Show answer

The mean. The large value is added into the sum, which pulls the mean up. The median moves at most one position.

4. A hiker walks 3.2 km. How many meters is that?

Show answer

3.2 × 1,000 = 3,200 m.

5. A bag holds 3 red, 5 blue, and 2 green beads. One bead is drawn without looking. What is the probability it is blue?

Show answer

Total = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10. P(blue) = 5/10 = 1/2, or 50%.

Reflection

  • Which of mean, median, mode, and range do you find easiest? Which one do you still need to slow down for?
  • Find a table or graph in a news story, on a food label, or in a weather app. What are its title and units, and what is one thing it shows?
  • Think of a time a single unusual value could give a misleading average (for example, one very high bill or one very hot day). Would the median tell a fairer story?

This Week's Study Plan (20–40 minutes a day)

DayTask
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Copy the mean, median, mode, and range table onto an index card. Redo the five Try It problems without looking. (25 min)
Day 2Complete practice items 1–6. For each one you miss, read the explanation and redo the calculation on paper. (30 min)
Day 3Complete practice items 7–12. Study the vocabulary list until you can define each term from memory. (30 min)
Day 4Collect your own data: record the outdoor temperature at the same time for five days, or your resting pulse five mornings in a row. Find the mean, median, mode, and range. Review the Study Notes. (20 min)
Day 5Take this week's Practice GED in Science under timed conditions. (90 min, may be split over two days)
Day 6Review every Practice GED question you missed. Sort your mistakes by type (misread data, wrong calculation, units, probability) and reread that part of the lesson. (30–40 min)

Test-Taking Strategy: Estimate Before You Calculate

Before you use the calculator, take five seconds to estimate. If the heart rates in a table are all between 60 and 90, the mean must be between 60 and 90, so an answer choice of 420 (the sum) or 15 is out. If a probability comes out greater than 1, you divided in the wrong order. Estimating catches the most common data mistakes and helps you eliminate wrong answer choices quickly.

vocab.def: Facts or measurements collected during an experiment or study.
vocab.example: The daily high temperatures recorded at a weather station.

vocab.def: An organized display of data in rows and columns with headings and units.
vocab.example: A table listing each day and that day's rainfall in inches.

vocab.def: A graph that uses bars to compare amounts in separate categories.
vocab.example: Bars showing the number of each tree species in a forest plot.

vocab.def: A graph that uses connected points to show how a quantity changes over time or with another quantity.
vocab.example: A line showing a patient's temperature every hour.

vocab.def: The overall direction of data: increasing, decreasing, or staying about the same.
vocab.example: Heart rate decreases steadily after exercise stops.

vocab.def: The average: the sum of the values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when the data are put in order. For an even number of values, the mean of the two middle values.
The value that appears most often in a data set.
The difference between the greatest and least values; a measure of spread.
vocab.example: For 58 to 88 bpm, the range is 30 bpm.

vocab.def: A value that is much higher or lower than the rest of the data.
vocab.example: Colony counts of 41, 44, 39, 42, and 104; 104 is an outlier.

vocab.def: A comparison of two quantities with different units, such as distance per time.
vocab.example: A sunflower growing 1.5 cm per day.

vocab.def: Changing a measurement from one unit to another without changing its size.
A number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
vocab.example: The probability of rolling a 6 on a fair number cube is 1/6.

vocab.def: The number of times an outcome is predicted to happen: probability times the number of tries.
vocab.example: With a 0.36 chance per trap, about 0.36 × 200 = 72 of 200 traps catch a mouse.

Read First: T-A-U-K

Title • Axes / headings • Units • Key

Bar graph = compare categories. Line graph = change over time. Steeper line = faster change. IV on x-axis, DV on y-axis.

Center and Spread

  • Mean = sum ÷ number of values
  • Median = middle of ordered data (even count: average the two middle values)
  • Mode = most frequent (can be none or more than one)
  • Range = greatest − least (spread, not center)

Outlier: pulls the mean; median barely moves. With an outlier, the median is usually the better "typical" value.

Rates

Rate = change in amount ÷ change in time
"per" means divide. Keep units: cm/day, bpm, mg/L.

Probability

P = favorable ÷ total (0 to 1)
P(not) = 1 − P
Expected = P × number of tries
1/4 = 0.25 = 25%

Temperature

°F = (°C × 9/5) + 32

LengthVolumeMassTime
1 cm = 10 mm; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 km = 1,000 m1 L = 1,000 mL1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 g = 1,000 mg1 min = 60 s; 1 h = 60 min

Big unit to small unit: multiply. Small unit to big unit: divide.

Example data: 58, 62, 68, 70, 74, 88 (bpm). Mean = 420 ÷ 6 = 70. Median = (68 + 70) ÷ 2 = 69. Mode = none. Range = 88 − 58 = 30.

Watch out: order data before finding the median • read the right row and units • total goes on the bottom of a probability • expected values are estimates • do not extend a trend far past the data.

items.prompt: What was the range of the daily high temperatures for the week?
items.hint: Range = greatest value minus least value.
items.explain:
The greatest high temperature was 87 °F (Sunday). The least was 74 °F (Friday).

Range = 87 − 74 = 13 °F.

87 °F is only the greatest value. 81 °F is the mean, which measures center, not spread. 74 °F is only the least value. The range always uses both: greatest minus least.

items.prompt: What was the mean daily high temperature for the week? Enter a number.
items.hint: Add all seven high temperatures, then divide by 7.
items.explain:
Add the seven high temperatures:

78 + 82 + 85 + 79 + 74 + 82 + 87 = 567

Divide by the number of days: 567 ÷ 7 = 81 °F.

A common error is dividing by 6 or forgetting one day. Check: 81 is between the least (74) and greatest (87) values, so it is reasonable.

items.prompt: Between which two consecutive minutes did the volunteer's heart rate drop the most?
items.hint: Subtract each heart rate from the one before it, or look for the steepest part of the line.
items.explain:
Find the drop for each minute:

  • 0 to 1: 150 − 132 = 18 bpm
  • 1 to 2: 132 − 118 = 14 bpm
  • 2 to 3: 118 − 106 = 12 bpm
  • 3 to 4: 106 − 98 = 8 bpm
  • 4 to 5: 98 − 92 = 6 bpm
  • 5 to 6: 92 − 88 = 4 bpm

The largest drop, 18 bpm, was between minute 0 and minute 1. That is the steepest part of the line. Minute 5 to minute 6 had the smallest drop; the line is flattening out there.

items.prompt: Which statements are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: The median high temperature is equal to the mode of the high temperatures.
The warmest day of the week was also the rainiest day.
The total rainfall for the week was 1.80 inches.
It rained on more than half of the days.
The mean high temperature was greater than the median high temperature.
The high temperature rose every day of the week.
items.hint: Order the temperatures to find the median and mode. Add the rainfall column.
items.explain:
Median and mode: In order, the highs are 74, 78, 79, 82, 82, 85, 87. The middle (4th) value is 82, so the median is 82 °F. The value 82 appears twice, so the mode is 82 °F. They are equal, so the statement that the median equals the mode is supported.

Total rainfall: 0.00 + 0.20 + 0.00 + 1.20 + 0.40 + 0.00 + 0.00 = 1.80 inches. Supported.

The others are not supported. The warmest day (Sunday, 87 °F) had no rain; Thursday was rainiest. It rained on only 3 of 7 days, which is less than half. The mean (81 °F) is less than the median (82 °F). The temperature fell on Thursday and Friday, so it did not rise every day.

items.prompt: What was the average rate at which the volunteer's heart rate decreased during the first 4 minutes after stopping?
items.hint: Rate of change = change in heart rate ÷ change in time. Use minute 0 and minute 4.
items.explain:
Heart rate at minute 0: 150 bpm. Heart rate at minute 4: 98 bpm.

Change in heart rate: 150 − 98 = 52 bpm.

Change in time: 4 − 0 = 4 minutes.

Rate: 52 ÷ 4 = 13 beats per minute, each minute.

52 is the total drop, not the rate per minute. 37.5 comes from 150 ÷ 4, and 24.5 comes from 98 ÷ 4; both divide a single reading by the time instead of dividing the change.

items.prompt:
A ruby-throated hummingbird's heart can beat about 1,200 times per minute while it is flying.

At that rate, its heart beats {{0}} times per second, and {{1}} times in one hour of flying.
items.hint: 1 minute = 60 seconds and 1 hour = 60 minutes. Going to a smaller unit of time means fewer beats; going to a larger unit means more.
items.explain:
Per second: A second is smaller than a minute, so there are fewer beats in it. 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20 beats per second.

Per hour: An hour is 60 minutes, so multiply: 1,200 × 60 = 72,000 beats.

Choosing 72,000 for the first blank multiplies when you should divide. 1,260 adds 60 instead of multiplying by it.

items.prompt: A scientist wants to display each data set below. Drag each data set into the type of graph that would display it best.
choices: A patient's body temperature recorded every hour for one day
The number of each kind of tree counted in a forest plot
The height of one sunflower measured every week for 10 weeks
The average yearly rainfall in four different cities
The level of carbon dioxide in the air measured each year from 2000 to 2020
The number of people with each blood type in a group of volunteers
items.hint: Does the data set show one thing changing over time, or does it compare separate categories?
items.explain:
Line graphs show how one quantity changes over time: body temperature each hour, sunflower height each week, and carbon dioxide level each year.

Bar graphs compare separate categories: kinds of trees, different cities, and blood types. There is no order in time connecting these categories, so connecting them with a line would suggest a trend that does not exist.

items.prompt: In a lesson on natural selection, a class models a beetle population with 20 beads in a bag: 6 brown, 9 green, and 5 yellow. A student draws one bead without looking. What is the probability that the bead is not green?
items.hint: Count the beads that are not green, then divide by the total number of beads.
items.explain:
Beads that are not green: 6 brown + 5 yellow = 11.

Total beads: 6 + 9 + 5 = 20.

P(not green) = 11 ÷ 20 = 0.55 = 55%.

You can also use the complement: P(green) = 9 ÷ 20 = 45%, so P(not green) = 100% − 45% = 55%. Choosing 45% gives the probability of drawing green, which is the opposite of what was asked. 30% is the probability of brown only, and 25% is the probability of yellow only.

items.prompt: A seed company's tests show that 85% of its tomato seeds sprout. A community garden plants 240 of these seeds. About how many seeds are expected to sprout? Enter a number.
items.hint: Expected number = probability × number of tries. Write 85% as a decimal first.
items.explain:
Write the percent as a decimal: 85% = 0.85.

Expected number = 0.85 × 240 = 204 seeds.

Check: 10% of 240 is 24, so 15% is 36. 240 − 36 = 204. A common error is computing the 15% that do not sprout (36) and stopping there.

items.prompt: The biologist wants one number that best describes the typical length of all six fish she caught. Which choice is best?
options: The median, 15.5 cm, because it is not pulled upward by the 45 cm fish
The mean, about 20.3 cm, because it is the only measure that uses every value
The range, 31 cm, because it includes both the shortest and longest fish
The mean of the shortest and longest fish, 29.5 cm, because it balances the extremes
items.hint: Look for an outlier. Which measure of center is affected least by one extreme value?
items.explain:
Fish 6 (45 cm) is an outlier: it is about three times as long as the others.

Median: In order: 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 45. The two middle values are 15 and 16. (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5 cm, which is close to five of the six fish.

Mean: 14 + 16 + 15 + 17 + 15 + 45 = 122; 122 ÷ 6 ≈ 20.3 cm. That is longer than five of the six fish, so it does not describe a typical fish; the outlier pulled it upward.

The range (45 − 14 = 31 cm) measures spread, not a typical value. The mean of the extremes, (14 + 45) ÷ 2 = 29.5 cm, is pulled even more by the outlier.

items.prompt: Based on the table, a randomly chosen person who was not vaccinated was about how many times as likely to be diagnosed with the flu as a randomly chosen person who was vaccinated?
items.hint: Find the probability of flu within each group by dividing by that group's total, not by 700. Then compare the two probabilities.
items.explain:
Find the probability of flu within each group:

  • Vaccinated: 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03 = 3%
  • Not vaccinated: 45 ÷ 300 = 0.15 = 15%

Compare: 15% ÷ 3% = 5 times as likely.

3.75 comes from 45 ÷ 12, which compares raw counts and ignores that the groups have different sizes (300 vs. 400). 12 comes from subtracting the percents (15 − 3), which gives a difference, not “how many times.” 1.3 comes from comparing the group totals (400 ÷ 300), which says nothing about the flu.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: As water temperature increases from 0 °C to 30 °C, the amount of dissolved oxygen the water can hold decreases.
For every 10 °C increase in temperature, dissolved oxygen decreases by the same amount.
Water at 40 °C would hold no dissolved oxygen.
Fish grow faster in warm water than in cold water.
items.hint: Check each statement against the numbers. For the statement about equal decreases, calculate each 10-degree change.
items.explain:
Every time the temperature goes up, dissolved oxygen goes down: 14.6 → 11.3 → 9.1 → 7.6 mg/L. So dissolved oxygen decreases as temperature increases over the range tested.

The decreases are not equal: 14.6 − 11.3 = 3.3; 11.3 − 9.1 = 2.2; 9.1 − 7.6 = 1.5 mg/L. The drops get smaller, so the line curves rather than falling by the same amount.

No data were collected at 40 °C, and the shrinking drops suggest the value would not reach 0, so that claim goes beyond the data. Fish growth was never measured, so the statement about fish growing faster in warm water is not supported.
